title: Mullin under scrutiny: the outages, the Iran report, and Wednesday's hearing
dek: The Homeland Security secretary has explained the FAA ground stop, a possible AI cause and a football trip in the same week CNN reported an Iranian dirty-bomb plan. Here is what is known and what is not.
body:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has spent the days since Friday's nationwide flight halt explaining things: the outage, the cause, the threat level, and his own weekend travel. Each explanation has drawn a new round of questions, from Democrats, from conservative commentators and, according to CNN, from inside the administration [1]. On Wednesday he is due to answer under oath before the House Homeland Security Committee at a worldwide threats hearing that was scheduled before any of this began. This report lays out what he has said, what is known and unknown about the outages, and where the new Iran intelligence fits [1].

## What happened Friday, and what Mullin said

The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a ground stop on departing flights across the country on Friday, Nov. 13. The Air Current's timeline, as summarized by the Wichita Liberty, puts the formal order at 3:44 p.m. Eastern and the lifting at 8:15 p.m. [6] CNN describes it as a four-hour stop; the gap is a matter of where one starts the clock. More than 3,500 aircraft were in the air when it began, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy [6].

Mullin, who does not run the FAA, was at the White House podium with Duffy that evening. Earlier, around 5 p.m., he had told reporters there was no sign of a cyberattack and called it a telecommunications outage [6]. He rejected comparisons to the Sept. 11 attacks, saying “that's a road I won't go down” [5]. At the later briefing he opened with a joke about the date and said the public “was never at danger” [1]. Duffy then blamed Congress for not funding an overhaul of the air traffic control system and warned of more breakdowns without the money, and Mullin joined the push for funding [1].

CNN reports that some administration officials were dumbfounded by the tone of the briefing and that others privately say Mullin was underprepared and has not been direct about the outages [1]. CNN also reported that the weekend's messaging left travelers without answers, which fed distrust of government [12].

## The explanations

The first question was whether the stop was an attack. On Friday Mullin said there was no indication of one. On Monday on Fox News he put it at 98 percent certainty that no cyberattack was involved [1]. He also told viewers the government's cybersecurity agency had told him the different outages were “all individually unrelated” [4].

The second question was the cause. Trump has said old and faulty equipment is to blame, and Duffy has framed the stop as proof of the need for modernization money [1]. On Monday Mullin offered a different idea, citing an unnamed person who is “very smart with tech”: that artificial intelligence might be overwhelming older systems [1]. CNN notes that he offered no technical evidence, and Democratic Rep. Ted Lieu answered on X that he would prefer facts before speculation [1].

There is a wrinkle in the AI theory. Three days before the stop, the FAA rolled out an AI-supported tool, the Strategic Management of Airspace system, known as SMART, to all 22 of its air route traffic control centers, according to the Washington Times as relayed by an ABC affiliate [7]. Asked on Friday whether that tool could have contributed, Mullin said “you can't rule out anything at this point,” according to Latin Times [8]. Nobody in the reporting available to The Watch has shown a link between SMART and the stop, and The Watch's Nov. 16 report on the FAA's own account points to a failed router rather than to AI. The root cause was still open as of that report. The responsible reading is that Mullin's AI theory is a theory, offered by an official who does not oversee the agency in question.

The third question was whether the outages are connected. CNN reported that a string of disruptions, including a Microsoft outage, the ground stop and a short United Airlines system failure, has fed conspiracy theories online [4][11]. Sen. James Lankford, an Oklahoma Republican, said on Fox News that the number of incidents demanded an investigation [11]. David Lapan, who was a Homeland Security spokesman in Trump's first term, told CNN the department has a credibility problem and cannot simply say there is nothing nefarious: it has to show its work [1]. A current DHS official told CNN the scrutiny is not about Mullin but about his predecessors, and that he is playing the hand he was dealt [1].

## The trip to Baton Rouge

The episode that has cost Mullin the most with allies is a flight. On Saturday he flew on a government plane to the LSU-Texas football game, about 21 hours after the ground stop was lifted, while airlines were still working through the backlog [1][12]. The weekend's stranded travelers included college football teams: Texas had boarded its own plane in Austin when the order came, then deplaned, and flew to Louisiana that night after the stop was lifted [9].

Mullin said in a CNBC interview that the trip would not have happened had the airways not been fully open for 21 hours, and that officials still have to live their lives [1]. He is required to fly on a government aircraft because of his job [1]. The explanation did not satisfy some on the right. Fox News commentator Tomi Lahren called him a “buffoon,” and radio host Todd Starnes called for his resignation [1].

## The Iran reporting

On Monday CNN reported, citing seven U.S. officials, that new intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans to target senior administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington [2][3]. Sources told CNN the planning is, for now, an effort by Iran to give itself options rather than a sign of an imminent attack, but that it has been specific, including locations and targets, and has set off U.S. contingency planning [2]. The White House said it is monitoring all potential threats and that there are currently no credible threats to the homeland [2].

Mullin said the threat is not new and described Iran's intentions as aspirational, while saying it is being taken seriously [3]. President Trump, speaking to reporters in the Philippines, said Iran would “pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before” if it attacked [3]. Mullin has added that a strike on Washington or another American city would cause “an all-out war” [1].

The Iran story and the outage story are separate, and CNN says plainly that none of the disruptions has been tied to each other [11]. They land on the same official in the same week, though, which is why the Wednesday hearing is likely to range widely.

## What to watch Wednesday

Mullin will testify alongside FBI deputy director Christopher Raia [1]. The questions he is likely to face fall into four groups:

- **Cause and coordination.** Who is in charge when a failure at one agency touches national security, and what did the cybersecurity agency actually find?
- **The AI theory.** Whether he can point to evidence, and whether SMART is being examined.
- **The Iran intelligence.** What protective steps have been taken for senior officials and for Washington.
- **The immigration crackdown.** Mullin has overseen two fatal shootings of immigrants by federal agents and has said the administration is not changing course after the midterms, while Trump told him to work with Democrats on reform; Mullin says amnesty is off the table [1].

Mullin took over the department in March after Kristi Noem was ousted, and had hoped to keep a low profile [1]. DHS says he surrounds himself with a strong leadership team and that anyone who says otherwise is trying to create the illusion of chaos [1]. The next two days will show whether lawmakers agree.
